leading_positions.synthesis: Five of eight round-1 files name B022 (optical lattice clocks, Katori and Ye) as the preferred single prize part, and all five propose the same two laureates. They differ in emphasis: Kroll, Lindroth and Pearce stress a measurement technique and independent cross-laboratory agreement at about 1e-18; Johansson and Olsson also stress derived physics results and the pending redefinition of the second. Citation wording is similar (magic-wavelength lattice, 1e-18 regime) but not identical. Johansson and Pearce moved to this position from a different opening first choice. All five list the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes as the main overlap risk, and all concede that Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, Lemonde and others are outside the two names. The five do not agree on whether the clock is a discovery or an invention, or on how strong the credit is: Kroll and Johansson call it the cleanest on the list, while Olsson, Lindroth and Pearce ask for expert checking of priority.

Two members prefer B045 (topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect) as the single prize part, both with the same trio, Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, and both with a citation built around the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators. Their shared case is a bulk topological invariant, theory followed by experiment in HgTe in 2007, and more than fifteen years of independent confirmation. Eriksson names B022 as his first alternative and says he would sooner see it awarded cleanly than force a contested trio; Mehlig lists B022 as his first alternative and calls it the safer prize if uncontested allocation is weighted above field-level influence. Olsson ranks B045 as an alternative but with Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan, a different laureate set that is not part of this position.

One member prefers B002 (baryon acoustic oscillations) with Eisenstein, Cole and Peacock, as a clean discovery from nature recovered independently in SDSS and 2dFGRS and by later surveys, and relevant to the current dark-energy debate. Danielsson states that this first place reflects his own weighting more than a committee view, and he would not block B022. No other member's configuration includes it.

areas_of_agreement: Every member who commented on B022 accepts it as a serious, mature candidate with reproduction across independent laboratories; no file argues against its science, and Danielsson and Eriksson say they would not oppose it.

Several members (Danielsson, Eriksson, Kroll, Lindroth, Mehlig, Olsson, Pearce, Johansson) note that the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 single-ion control prizes must be addressed in any lattice-clock citation, and that the citation should name the magic-wavelength lattice rather than clocks in general.

Danielsson, Kroll, Lindroth, Mehlig, Olsson and Johansson name the missing Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang or Girvin and Devoret credit, or the SDSS and 2dFGRS collaboration problem, as unresolved attribution problems for B045, B039 and B002. Several of them also say they are relying on memory for credit history and want documentary checking.

Johansson, Kroll, Lindroth, Mehlig and Olsson all say that a second superconducting-circuit prize one year after the 2025 prize (B039, B032) is hard to justify, and that the transmon and Girvin and Devoret credit complicates B039; Danielsson raises the same two concerns, and Johansson has himself moved B039 down.
No file proposes a multi-part prize; all eight preferred configurations contain a single part with two or three laureates.
scientific_disputes: Discovery versus instrument: Danielsson and Mehlig regard the lattice clock as a superb measurement advance but ask whether it tells us something unexpected about nature (limits on drifting constants and dark matter are so far limits, not detections), while Lindroth, Olsson, Johansson, Kroll and Pearce answer that new regimes (many-atom control, millimetre-scale redshift) are physics results in their own right.

Mehlig describes the lattice clock as an application of known atomic physics (magic-wavelength trapping, Lamb-Dicke confinement) and places the conceptual novelty of a classifying invariant above a smaller uncertainty budget; Lindroth, Olsson and Pearce hold that using many atoms with no first-order light shift was not obviously possible.

Whether the 2016 topological-phases prize leaves room for B045: Eriksson argues it covered a different discovery (defects, phase transitions, Haldane), while Mehlig calls the distinction defensible but not self-evident, and Danielsson and Pearce flag it as an overlap.

IceCube (B046) is a first or high ranking for Pearce and Danielsson ranks it fourth, but Lindroth and Olsson note that source identification is limited to a few objects and that independent confirmation by another detector is thinner than for the clock; Pearce concedes the latter.

Whether a third cosmology prize after 2006, 2011 and 2019 is acceptable for B002 (Danielsson, Eriksson and Olsson raise it), and whether recent DESI results on evolving dark energy strengthen or complicate the case.
attribution_disputes: B022: Katori and Ye are accepted as the pair by the five supporters and by Mehlig, but Ludlow, Takamoto, Hinkley, Lemonde, Ovsiannikov and others are outside the names. Kroll treats Takamoto's work as covered by Katori; Olsson and Lindroth would not dismiss Lemonde, Ludlow and Hinkley so lightly and want the early strontium lattice papers checked.

B045: the same trio (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) is proposed by Eriksson and Mehlig, but Olsson proposes Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan, dropping Mele. Eriksson and Mehlig reply that dropping Mele removes half of the Z2 theory, while Olsson argues the trio credits theory twice and leaves out the first 3D ARPES observation. The BHZ proposal (Zhang deceased) and the 3D theorists (Fu, Moore, Balents, Roy) are outside every proposed trio.

B002: Danielsson names Eisenstein, Cole and Peacock, but Kroll, Lindroth, Mehlig, Olsson and Pearce object that two large survey collaborations made the detection and that Peebles and Yu and Sunyaev and Zeldovich predicted the feature, so a trio is partly arbitrary.

B046: Pearce credits Halzen and Karle, but Kroll, Lindroth and Olsson ask how two names can represent a roughly 300-person collaboration with AMANDA and DUMAND precursors; Pearce accepts that expert documentation of individual roles is needed.

B039 and B033 (named in alternatives): B039 omits Girvin and Devoret, and B033 raises the question whether the unit is the Cirac-Zoller proposal or the experiments (Innsbruck, NIST, Monroe), with Wineland's 2012 prize overlapping.

B027 (Mehlig's opening first choice, not in any preferred configuration): priority among Evans, Cohen, Morriss, Gallavotti, Kurchan and others is contested, and the experimental verifications are by people not credited.
maturity_disputes: B022: whether the committee should wait for the redefinition of the second. Olsson, Johansson, Kroll, Lindroth and Pearce each list this as an uncertainty, and Pearce, Kroll and Lindroth say that scientific recognition does not need to wait; Danielsson says the redefinition belongs to metrology, not to the prize criterion.

B045: Eriksson and Mehlig regard it as mature, with fifteen years of independent transport and ARPES confirmation across HgTe, Bi-Sb and Bi2Se3-class materials; Pearce and Danielsson regard the maturity as not in doubt but give priority to the credit problem; applications remain modest.

B046: the diffuse flux is repeatedly confirmed within IceCube, but source population for most of it is unresolved, and independent confirmation from KM3NeT or Baikal is thinner (Pearce, Olsson, Lindroth).
B030 (alternative of Eriksson and Olsson): Eriksson currently judges magic-angle graphene too early because of the pairing-mechanism debate and twist-angle disorder.
conflict_or_recusal_flags: Johansson (B039, B032): directs the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and works in superconducting circuits, with close Chalmers ties to Delsing and Wilson (co-authors on the dynamical Casimir effect) and co-authored work on phonons coupled to artificial atoms; he would recuse himself from the discussion of B039's ranking in a final decision, and he notes the Chalmers hosting of 2025 laureates.

Kroll (B022): spent a year in John Hall's laboratory (Hall, 2005 laureate, worked closely with JILA, where Jun Ye is active) and leads quantum sensing in WACQT and a slow-light filter company; he reports no co-authorship with Ye or Katori, believes this does not require recusal, and asks that it be noted to the chair.

Pearce (chair, B046): field adjacency in astroparticle physics and an opening first-place ranking of B046 that should be weighed; no recorded collaboration with IceCube or the credited names; he also notes that his role as Chair is relevant.

Danielsson (B002) and Eriksson (B045): both state same-broad-field interest (dark-energy and de Sitter research; topological band theory and electronic structure) but no personal or institutional tie to any credited name.

Lindroth: collaborator of Anne L'Huillier and atomic physics adjacency to B047, with no known tie to any B022 name. Mehlig: same Gothenburg physics environment as Johansson and Olsson, no known tie to credited candidates.
Olsson: no tie to any credited name but notes Johansson's declared interest in B039 and B032.
questions_for_round2: B022: does the committee accept that the magic-wavelength many-atom lattice is a distinct invention from the 2005 comb and the 2012 single-ion prizes, and can supporters agree on one citation that names the lattice and the 1e-18 regime and not clocks in general?

B022: do the early strontium lattice papers (Takamoto and Katori 2005, Ludlow and Ye, Lemonde's group, Hinkley) and the magic-wavelength proposal support Katori for concept and first demonstration and Ye for performance, and is a two-name prize defensible, as asked by Kroll, Lindroth, Olsson and Pearce?

B045: if the committee wants a topological prize, is the unit the 2D quantum spin Hall effect (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) or topological insulators generally, which would bring in Hasan, and how should the 2016 topological-phases prize and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal be handled in the citation?
B045: can Eriksson and Mehlig, and Olsson, resolve whether Mele or Hasan is in a three-name configuration, and does either variant survive the contested 3D credit (Fu, Moore, Balents, Roy)?

B045 versus B022: Eriksson and Mehlig each name B022 as their first alternative. Under what condition, for instance if the topological credit cannot be settled with documentation, would they support B022, and is there any remaining substantive objection to it that is not about the overlap with 2005 and 2012?

B002 and B046: what documentary evidence would Danielsson offer on who the discoverers are (SDSS, 2dFGRS, theory predecessors), and what evidence would Pearce offer on Halzen's and Karle's decisive roles, given Kroll's stated requirement for this before B046 could rank above B022?

Would the committee wait for the redefinition of the second before any award on B022, and does Danielsson's criterion that clocks yield clues from nature, rather than limits, apply with the same weight to other measurement-led candidates?

Should the committee treat any second superconducting-circuit prize (B039, B032) as ruled out for 2026 by the 2025 prize, and how should the declared conflicts of Johansson (B039, B032) and Kroll (B022) be handled in round 2 and the final ballot?
summary.chair_observation: On the explicit round-1 files, B022 is the preferred single prize part of five of eight members with an identical two-name configuration, B045 of two members with an identical trio, and B002 of one. No other ballot appears as a preferred configuration. The B022 support is accompanied by shared caveats on overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes and on uncredited groups, not by objections to the science, while B045 supporters themselves describe the credit as unresolved and name B022 as their first alternative. Two of the five B022 supporters, Johansson and Pearce, say they changed their first choice after reading the other files. These counts are only of stated positions, and round 2 should test the attribution and citation questions above before any ranking is drawn.
